title: Module Documentation: Turán's Hypergraph Problem
content: The module docstring frames Problem #500 as one of the most famous open problems in extremal combinatorics. It states the central question: determine $\text{ex}_3(n, K_4^{(3)})$, the maximum number of 3-element subsets of an $n$-element set that avoid containing all four 3-subsets of any 4-element set. Turán's 1941 construction (3-partition) gives $(5/9 + o(1))\binom{n}{3}$ edges, Razborov's 2010 flag algebra bound gives $\leq 0.5612\binom{n}{3}$. Erdős considered this important enough to assign it Problem #500 with a \$500 prize.
mathContext: $\text{ex}_3(n, K_4^{(3)}) = \max\{|E| : E \subseteq \binom{[n]}{3},\; \forall S \in \binom{[n]}{4},\; \exists T \in \binom{S}{3},\; T \notin E\}$. Turán conjecture: $\lim_{n \to \infty} \text{ex}_3(n)/\binom{n}{3} = 5/9$.

title: Imports and Dependencies
content: Imports $\texttt{SimpleGraph.Basic}$ (for graph-theoretic context), $\texttt{Finset.Basic}$ (for hyperedge collections), $\texttt{Nat.Choose.Basic}$ (for binomial coefficients $\binom{n}{3}$), and $\texttt{Tactic}$ for proof automation.
mathContext: The formalization represents 3-uniform hypergraphs as $\texttt{Finset}(\texttt{Finset}(\texttt{Fin}\ n))$ and uses $\texttt{Nat.choose}\ n\ 3 = \binom{n}{3}$ for the total number of triples.

title: 3-Uniform Hypergraph
content: A 3-uniform hypergraph on vertex set $\texttt{Fin}\ n$ is a collection of 3-element subsets (edges). Unlike ordinary graphs (2-uniform), hyperedges connect triples of vertices. The type $\texttt{Hypergraph3}(n) = \texttt{Finset}(\texttt{Finset}(\texttt{Fin}\ n))$ allows arbitrary edge collections; 3-uniformity is enforced by $\texttt{IsThreeUniform}$.

title: 3-Uniformity Predicate
content: The predicate $\texttt{IsThreeUniform}$ requires every edge $e \in H$ to have exactly 3 vertices ($e.\text{card} = 3$). This is the higher-dimensional analogue of requiring all edges in a graph to be pairs.

title: $K_4^{(3)}$ Containment
content: $K_4^{(3)}$ is the complete 3-uniform hypergraph on 4 vertices, containing all $\binom{4}{3} = 4$ triples. Containment means there exist 4 vertices $S$ with $|S| = 4$ such that every 3-subset of $S$ is an edge. This is the simplest forbidden subhypergraph whose Turán density is unknown.
mathContext: $\texttt{ContainsK4\_3}(H) \iff \exists S \subseteq V,\; |S| = 4 \wedge \forall T \in \binom{S}{3},\; T \in E(H)$. Note: $|K_4^{(3)}| = \binom{4}{3} = 4$ edges.

title: $K_4^{(3)}$-Free Hypergraph
content: A $K_4^{(3)}$-free hypergraph is 3-uniform and contains no 4 vertices spanning all 4 triples. Equivalently, every 4-vertex set misses at least one triple. The extremal problem asks: how many edges can such a hypergraph have?

title: Turán Number $\text{ex}_3(n, K_4^{(3)})$
content: The Turán number $\text{ex}_3(n, K_4^{(3)})$ is the maximum number of edges in a $K_4^{(3)}$-free 3-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices. Axiomatized with achievability (some hypergraph attains it) and optimality (no hypergraph exceeds it).
mathContext: $\text{ex}_3(n, K_4^{(3)}) = \max\{|E(H)| : H \text{ is } K_4^{(3)}\text{-free on } n \text{ vertices}\}$.

title: Achievability and Optimality Axioms
content: Two axioms formalize the extremal property: `ex3_K4_achievable` guarantees existence (some $K_4^{(3)}$-free hypergraph attains $\text{ex}_3(n)$ edges), and `ex3_K4_optimal` guarantees maximality (no $K_4^{(3)}$-free hypergraph exceeds it). Together they characterize $\text{ex}_3(n)$ as a maximum rather than a supremum — the extremal hypergraph exists for every $n$. This is guaranteed by compactness of the space of hypergraphs on $n$ vertices.
mathContext: $\exists H : |E(H)| = \text{ex}_3(n) \wedge H \text{ is } K_4^{(3)}\text{-free}$ (achievability) and $\forall H : H \text{ is } K_4^{(3)}\text{-free} \Rightarrow |E(H)| \leq \text{ex}_3(n)$ (optimality).

title: Turán Density $\pi(K_4^{(3)})$
content: The Turán density $\pi(K_4^{(3)}) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \text{ex}_3(n, K_4^{(3)})/\binom{n}{3}$ exists by the Katona–Nemetz–Simonovits theorem (1964), which guarantees convergence for all hypergraph Turán problems. The axiom formalizes $\pi$ as a real number with an $\varepsilon$-$N$ convergence statement.

title: Turán's Lower Bound: $\pi \geq 5/9$ (1941)
content: Turán's elegant construction: partition $n$ vertices into 3 nearly-equal parts $V_1, V_2, V_3$. Include all triples $\{a, b, c\}$ that intersect each part in at most 2 vertices (equivalently, not all 3 from one part). This gives $(5/9 + o(1))\binom{n}{3}$ edges and is $K_4^{(3)}$-free since any 4 vertices spanning all triples would require 2 in the same part.
mathContext: $\pi(K_4^{(3)}) \geq 5/9$. Construction: $E = \{\{a,b,c\} : \text{not all 3 in same part}\}$. Edge count: $\binom{n}{3} - 3\binom{n/3}{3} = (5/9+o(1))\binom{n}{3}$.

title: Razborov's Upper Bound: $\pi \leq 0.5612$ (2010)
content: Alexander Razborov used his flag algebra method to prove $\pi(K_4^{(3)}) \leq 0.5611666\ldots$, dramatically improving earlier bounds. De Caen (1994) had $\pi \leq 1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707$. Flag algebras encode density inequalities as semidefinite programs, providing rigorous computer-assisted bounds. The gap $5/9 \approx 0.5556$ to $0.5612$ is small but stubbornly unresolved.

title: Turán's Conjecture: $\pi(K_4^{(3)}) = 5/9$
content: Turán conjectured in 1941 that his 3-partition construction is optimal: $\pi(K_4^{(3)}) = 5/9$. After 80+ years, this remains one of the most famous and stubborn open problems in combinatorics. Erdős offered \$500 for its resolution (hence Problem #500). Unlike the graph Turán theorem (solved by Turán himself for $K_r$), the hypergraph case has resisted all approaches.

title: Exact Values for Small $n$
content: Known exact values: $\text{ex}_3(4, K_4^{(3)}) = 3$ (out of $\binom{4}{3} = 4$ possible), $\text{ex}_3(5, K_4^{(3)}) = 7$ (out of 10), $\text{ex}_3(6, K_4^{(3)}) = 13$ (out of 20). All consistent with Turán's conjecture. Computing $\text{ex}_3(n)$ for $n \geq 7$ is computationally challenging.

title: Current Bounds Summary
content: The combined bounds $5/9 \leq \pi(K_4^{(3)}) \leq 0.5612$ form the tightest known interval. The gap of $\approx 0.0056$ has narrowed dramatically since de Caen's 1994 bound of $1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707$, but closing it entirely remains one of the great challenges of extremal combinatorics.
